## LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by the Legislature

Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. **Fiscal Impact:** Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. **Supporters:** California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce **Opponents:** California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.

### WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS

YES A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

 

### ARGUMENTS

PRO Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.

CON PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"California Proposition 43 2026 voter guide","content":"**California Proposition 43 (November 3, 2026 ballot)** is a legislatively referred constitutional amendment that would raise the voter-approval threshold for certain local special taxes.[[1]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)

It is titled “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.” It was placed on the ballot by the Legislature (ACA 22) with strong bipartisan support (Assembly 68-2, Senate 35-1).[[1]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)

### Official Title and Summary (Attorney General)
Currently, local governments must obtain two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) that they place on the ballot. However, this two-thirds vote requirement does not currently apply to special taxes put on the ballot by voter signature gathering.

This measure would limit voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by raising the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds. It applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027.[[1]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)

It would also prohibit local governments (including via initiative) from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property except as already allowed under the California Constitution.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_43)

### What Your Vote Means
- **YES**: Certain local government taxes (voter-proposed special taxes) would require two-thirds approval by voters.
- **NO**: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.[[3]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/43.htm)

### Fiscal Impact (Legislative Analyst’s Office)
Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. The actual impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.[[4]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)

### Background
Proposition 13 (1978) generally requires a two-thirds vote for local special taxes (those earmarked for a specific purpose, such as sales taxes, parcel taxes, or utility taxes dedicated to particular services). A 2017 California Supreme Court decision (*California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland*) and subsequent appellate rulings created a distinction: special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments still need two-thirds, but those placed via citizen initiative (signature gathering) can pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close this distinction starting in 2027, restoring a uniform two-thirds requirement for voter-initiated special taxes. It originated as a legislative compromise that kept a broader Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association initiative off the ballot.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_43)

Examples of past measures that passed with a majority but would have needed two-thirds under this proposal include some local sales taxes for emergency services and real estate transfer taxes (sometimes called “mansion taxes”).

### Arguments in Favor
Supporters (including the California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association) argue it restores Proposition 13 taxpayer protections, closes court-created loopholes that have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes, protects homeowners/renters/small businesses from costly new real estate, sales, and utility taxes, and ensures broad voter support plus accountability for how tax dollars are spent. They note over 2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade.[[5]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)

### Arguments Against
Opponents (including California Professional Firefighters, California Federation of Teachers, Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA, and housing/environmental groups) argue it limits voters’ ability to fund essential local services like fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals, and affordable housing. They say it lets a 33.4% minority veto what a majority wants, does not cut existing taxes, and benefits corporate interests over communities. They emphasize that majority rule should apply to local voter decisions.[[5]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)

### Official Resources
The full Official Voter Information Guide (including complete arguments, rebuttals, analysis, and proposed text) is available at voterguide.sos.ca.gov. Key pages:
- Title and Summary
- Quick Reference Guide
- Arguments and Rebuttals
- Analysis by the Legislative Analyst

## LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

### ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43

VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT

California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.

We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS

Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.

PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES

Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes—using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.

These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.

Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.

PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES

California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.

Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.

Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.

PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS

Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety—only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.

If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.

PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE

Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.

Vote YES on Prop. 43:

• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.

**Robert Gutierrez**, President  
 California Taxpayers Association  
 **Robert Rivinius**, President  
 Family Business Association of California  
 **Julian Canete**, President  
 California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43

We all want relief from California’s high cost of living. But Proposition 43 doesn’t cut your taxes a penny. It attacks something far more valuable: the power of your vote.

PROP. 43 WEAKENS YOUR VOTE.

Today, when local voters decide how to fund their communities, the majority rules. Prop. 43 throws that out, letting just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Under Prop. 43, a NO vote counts twice as much as a YES. That isn’t fair, and it isn’t democracy.

PROP. 43 DEEPENS THE HOUSING CRISIS.

Across California, communities vote to build affordable homes for working families, seniors, and veterans. They are helping renters stay housed and move people off the streets. Prop. 43 hands a small minority the power to block those solutions, even when a clear majority of your neighbors support them.

PROP. 43 TIES YOUR COMMUNITY’S HANDS.

Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund the critical local services your community counts on: staffing fire stations and 911 response, preparing neighborhoods for wildfire, repairing crumbling roads, keeping schools, parks, and libraries open, and protecting local hospitals and clinics as Washington cuts healthcare funding. When funding is blocked, help arrives slower, classrooms grow more crowded, and communities are left less safe.

KEEP THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS—WITH YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBORS.

That’s why teachers, nurses, firefighters, and housing advocates all oppose Prop. 43.

VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.

*www.NoProp43CA.com*

**Nick Lapis**, Director of Advocacy  
 Californians Against Waste  
 **Bill Barnes**, Director of Campaigns & Community  
 Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California  
 **Steve Frisch**, President  
 Sierra Business Council

### ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 43

PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.

Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts. Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions—and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.

PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.

Local police and firefighters can’t rely on Sacramento or Washington politicians. These services are funded at the local level. Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. Without adequate funding, 911 response times are slower, fire stations sit understaffed, and families wait longer for help when every second counts. When a house fire breaks out—or a wildfire threatens our neighborhoods—that local funding is what protects us. Prop. 43 would let a small minority of voters block it. Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services.

PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.

Across California, local voters have come together to repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local hospitals and healthcare—especially as Washington cuts federal health funding. These are decisions communities make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43 hands a small group of voters the power to veto those solutions, even when the majority supports them.

PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY.

In America, we believe in one person, one vote—and the majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want. It puts the out-voted minority in charge—even if they are extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote.

CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.

Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold these corporations and developers accountable at the ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away—to protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.

That’s why these organizations are asking you to vote NO on Prop. 43:

• California Professional Firefighters • Californians Against Waste • California Federation of Teachers • California School Employees Association • Communities for a Better Environment • AAPI Force • Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California • Nurses Alliance of SEIU California • Sierra Business Council

Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the power where it belongs—with you and your neighbors.

VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.

*www.NoProp43CA.com*

**Darrell Roberts**, President  
 California Professional Firefighters  
 **Chris Harkins**, Executive Director  
 Nurse Alliance of SEIU California  
 **Adam Weinberger**, President  
 California School Employees Association

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST  
PROPOSITION 43

VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS

Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire, local politicians waste your money on their pet projects— then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the most important priorities.

The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions in taxes they should not have had to pay.

Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas, and real estate taxes.

Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on new or higher local taxes and requires governments to spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters approved—preventing bait-and-switch schemes that make our sky-high cost of living even worse.

Over the last decade, local governments have imposed 2,000 new or higher taxes. Prop. 43 CLOSES LOOPHOLES used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases, restores the protections voters originally approved under Proposition 13, and makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes without broad voter support.

The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot sends a clear message: activist courts exceeded voters’ intent by creating loopholes that weakened Proposition 13’s protections.

Restore your right to vote on ALL local taxes.

VOTE YES ON PROP. 43

## LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

  

### OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY

### PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL

*   Currently, local governments must obtain two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) that they place on the ballot. However, this two-thirds vote requirement does not currently apply to special taxes put on ballot by voter signature gathering.
*   This measure would limit voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by raising the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds.
*   Applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027.

### SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:

*   Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.

Proposition 43 (2026)

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Flag_of_California.svg/60px-Flag_of_California.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)* * *

**November 3, 2026**

**Restoration Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Initiative Special Taxes Amendment**

**Proposition 43** is a proposed [legislative constitutional amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_amendment "Constitutional amendment") on the November 3, 2026, ballot in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California").

Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under [Proposition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_California_Proposition_13 "1978 California Proposition 13") for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local [initiative power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_initiative "Popular initiative").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the [California Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California "Constitution of California").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)

Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the [California Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_California "Supreme Court of California"),[\[3\]](#cite_note-Upland-3) which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13. These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

Proposition 43 was placed on the ballot by [legislative referral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_referral "Legislative referral")[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) with bipartisan support from both Democrats and Republicans in the [California State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") by a 68–2 vote in the [California State Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Assembly "California State Assembly") and by a 35–1 vote in the [California State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Senate "California State Senate").[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

## Background

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")\]

On three previous occasions, California voters approved the two-thirds voter approval requirement for all local special taxes when they adopted the Proposition 13 initiative constitutional amendment in 1978, the Proposition 62 statutory initiative in 1986, and the [Proposition 218](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_California_Proposition_218 "1996 California Proposition 218") (“Right to Vote on Taxes Act”) initiative constitutional amendment in 1996.

In 1987, a California appellate court in the *Altadena Library* case held that the two-thirds voter approval requirement for local special taxes under Proposition 13 *applied* to a local initiative special tax increase proposed by the electorate under the local initiative power.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The *Altadena Library* case was later cited with approval by the California Supreme Court in a 1995 case upholding the statutory voter approval requirements for local taxes under Proposition 62 (a 1986 taxpayer protection initiative measure), including the two-thirds voter approval requirement for local special taxes.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Following the *Altadena Library* case, California law was clear for decades that local special tax initiatives were subject to two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13.

### 2017 *Upland* decision and later court rulings

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 2017 Upland decision and later court rulings")\]

In the 2017 [*Upland* case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_California_Proposition_218#Application_of_Proposition_218_to_local_tax_initiatives_\(2017_Upland_decision\) "1996 California Proposition 218") relating to Proposition 218 (“Right to Vote on Taxes Act”—a constitutional follow-up to Proposition 13), a divided California Supreme Court created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the voter approval requirements under constitutional taxpayer protection laws such as Proposition 13.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Upland-3)

The *Upland* decision was controversial and had an extensive dissenting opinion written by Justice [Leondra Kruger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leondra_Kruger "Leondra Kruger") and joined by Justice [Goodwin Liu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwin_Liu "Goodwin Liu"), both of whom were appointed by former Democratic Governor [Jerry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Brown "Jerry Brown").[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) In her dissenting opinion, Justice Kruger wrote that the voters never intended to distinguish between taxes placed on the ballot by the governing body and those proposed under the initiative power so as to create an exemption from Proposition 13 voter approval requirements for special tax increases proposed under the local initiative power.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

Local special taxes placed on the ballot by a local governing body such as a city council or a county board of supervisors are subject to two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) However, the majority opinion in th*e Upland* case contained ambiguous language on whether or not the two-thirds vote requirement under Proposition 13 applied to citizen-led special tax initiatives. This ambiguity led to lower appellate courts subsequently ruling that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13 does *not* apply to citizen-led initiatives.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) To date, the California Supreme Court has refused to clarify the ambiguous language contained in its 2017 *Upland* decision or to resolve the conflict with the 1987 *Altadena Library* case which applied the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13 to a local initiative special tax.

For special tax measures proposed under the local initiative power, the *Upland* decision took away from voters their constitutional right to vote on local special taxes under Proposition 13, a constitutional right that was previously recognized in the 1987 *Altadena Library* case.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) The primary purpose of Proposition 43 is to restore that constitutional right to vote under Proposition 13 for special taxes proposed under the local initiative power.

As a result of the appellate court rulings following the *Upland* decision, many local initiative special tax increases passed *without* two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13. These include the Measure ULA (2022) “mansion tax” in [Los Angeles,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles")[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) the Proposition C business tax in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco,_CA "San Francisco, CA"), and numerous local sales and property tax increases. 

### Proposed initiative constitutional amendment

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Proposed initiative constitutional amendment")\]

In response to local special tax increases imposed without two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13, an initiative constitutional amendment known as the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” was filed and later obtained sufficient signatures to appear on the November 2026 statewide ballot in California.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)

The “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative contained several integrated components that included: (1) restoring the two-thirds vote requirement under Proposition 13 for special taxes proposed under the local initiative power; (2) significantly limiting the ability of local governments to impose real property transfer taxes like the Measure ULA "mansion tax" in Los Angeles; (3) ending existing initiative parcel taxes enacted without two-thirds voter approval; and (4) ending existing real property transfer taxes levied in [charter cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_rule_in_the_United_States#Home_rule_charter_cities "Home rule in the United States"), including the Measure ULA “mansion tax” in Los Angeles.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)

### Proposition 43 bipartisan compromise

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Proposition 43 bipartisan compromise")\]

Ultimately, a bipartisan compromise was reached that resulted in the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative being withdrawn from the ballot by the initiative proponent[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) in favor of a more limited proposed constitutional amendment (ACA 22) that was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature and became known as Proposition 43.

Under the Proposition 43 bipartisan compromise, only the measure that would restore the two-thirds vote requirement under Proposition 13 for special taxes proposed under the local initiative power will appear on the November 2026 ballot for California voters to decide. Other components of the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative would not appear on the November 2026 ballot, including the limitations on real property transfer taxes and the provisions ending any already existing local taxes, including the Measure ULA “mansion tax” in Los Angeles.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) In exchange for withdrawing the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative, the Legislature also agreed to remove another proposed legislative constitutional amendment from the ballot (ACA 13) that would have made taxpayer protection constitutional amendments containing supermajority vote requirements much harder for California voters to approve.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)

# **Proposition 43**

Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.

* * *

## Analysis of Measure

### Background

***Local Governments in California.*** California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.

***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.

### Proposal

***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

### Fiscal Effects

***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

* * *

## Yes/No Statement

A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.

A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

* * *

## Summary of Legislative Analyst’s Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact

*   Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.

* * *

## Ballot Label

**Fiscal Impact**: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.

This closes a distinction created by post-2017 court rulings (following the California Supreme Court’s *Upland* decision), under which government-placed special taxes already need two-thirds approval but citizen-initiated ones can pass with a simple majority. The Legislative Analyst’s Office notes a possible reduction in future local tax revenues, though the amount is unknown and depends on future voter and government decisions. It does not affect existing taxes or general (non-earmarked) taxes.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_43)

Independent analyses from the requested sources (plus related nonpartisan ones like the LAO) generally describe it as restoring uniformity to Proposition 13-era rules but raising concerns about majority rule, local funding flexibility, and equity. Polling from PPIC shows it trailing.

### League of Women Voters of California
The LWV (via its Education Fund Easy Voter Guide and “Vote with the League” recommendations) provides a straightforward, nonpartisan explanation and recommends **No**. Current law allows citizen-initiated special taxes (for schools, roads, parks, public safety, etc.) to pass with a majority, while government-placed ones need two-thirds. Prop 43 would apply the two-thirds threshold uniformly starting in 2027 (including extensions) and bar most new property-value taxes via initiative. The League opposes it because it “would let a minority of voters block tax measures supported by most voters and make it harder for communities to raise revenue when local needs or economic conditions change.” They emphasize it weakens majority rule without cutting existing taxes.[[2]](https://cavotes.org/easy-voter-guide/accessible/)

### PPIC (Public Policy Institute of California)
PPIC’s independent statewide surveys (nonpartisan polling, not a full policy brief) show consistent opposition among likely voters. In September 2026: 43% yes, 51% no. In October 2026 (Oct. 16–22): 42% yes, 55% no (with 3% undecided). Support is higher among Republicans (around 68%) than Democrats (28%) or independents (41%), and among older voters; it is below 50% across regions.  **California Proposition 43**, the **Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment**, is on the [ballot](/California_2026_ballot_measures "California 2026 ballot measures") in [California](/California "California") as a [legislatively referred constitutional amendment](/Legislatively_referred_constitutional_amendment "Legislatively referred constitutional amendment") on [November 3, 2026](/California_2026_ballot_measures "California 2026 ballot measures").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Overview-1)[\[2\]](#cite_note-Text-2) 

A "**yes**" vote supports this amendment to:

*   require that local ballot measures proposing, extending, or increasing special taxes initiated by citizens receive a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to be enacted and
*   prohibit local jurisdictions and ballot initiatives from enacting ad valorem property taxes, except for voter-approved bond debt-service taxes authorized elsewhere in the state constitution.

A "**no**" vote opposes this amendment to require that local ballot measures proposing, extending, or increasing special taxes initiated by citizens receive a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to be enacted, thereby maintaining that only a simple majority vote (50%+1) is required to enact initiated local special taxes.

## Overview

### How would Proposition 43 change the vote requirements for local special tax initiatives?

*See also: [Text of measure](#Text_of_measure)*

The initiative would amend the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution") to require that local ballot measures proposing, extending, or increasing special taxes initiated by citizens receive a [two-thirds (66.67%) vote](/Supermajority_requirement "Supermajority requirement") to be enacted. Currently, local special tax measures can be enacted in two ways: 1) a local governing board sends the tax to voters, and it is approved by a two-thirds vote, or 2) citizens can petition to place a special tax on local ballots, and it is approved by a simple majority of voters.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Text-2) 

The amendment would also prohibit any local government from levying ad valorem taxes on real property, including by ballot initiative, except for those authorized under [Article XIII](/Article_XIII,_California_Constitution "Article XIII, California Constitution") and [Article XIII A](/Article_XIII_A,_California_Constitution "Article XIII A, California Constitution"), which establishes a 1% base tax on real property and authorizes additional voter-approved bond debt-service property taxes.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Text-2) 

### How did Proposition 43 get on the ballot?

*See also: [Path to the ballot](#Path_to_the_ballot)*

Proposition 43 was placed on the ballot as part of a legislative compromise between Democratic state leaders and petitioners sponsoring [another initiative](/California_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Special_Taxes_and_Charter_City_Real_Estate_Transfer_Tax_Prohibition_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)") that would have increased the vote requirement to pass citizen-initiated local special taxes from a simple majority to a two-thirds vote; prohibited charter cities from imposing their own real estate transfer taxes, whether for general or specific purposes, above the existing statutory rate of $0.275 per $500 of value; and invalidated any property-related special taxes previously adopted with an approval rate below two-thirds or real estate transfer taxes in charter cities. California state law allows initiative sponsors to withdraw qualified initiatives until the ballot finalization deadline, which is 131 days before the election. The initiative was withdrawn from the ballot after the [California State Legislature](/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") passed [Proposition 43](#Path_to_the_ballot) on June 25 — the 2026 ballot finalization deadline. It passed the state Assembly by a vote of 68-2, with nine not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 35-1, with four not voting.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Overview-1) 

### What are supporters and opponents saying about Proposition 43?

*See also: [Support](#Support) and [Opposition](#Opposition)*

Jon Coupal, president of Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which sponsored the [withdrawn initiative](#California_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Special_Taxes_and_Charter_City_Real_Estate_Transfer_Tax_Prohibition_Initiative_\(2026\)), said, "In 2024, the California Legislature sought to make it easier to raise taxes with Proposition 5, which the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association defeated at the ballot. Today the Legislature voted to make it harder to raise taxes by advancing a constitutional amendment, ACA 22, to close a loophole that had allowed some special taxes to pass with less than the two-thirds vote required by Proposition 13."[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) 

State Asm. [Buffy Wicks](/Buffy_Wicks "Buffy Wicks") (D-14), who authored Proposition 43, came out in opposition to the amendment. She said, "I authored ACA 22 not because I wanted it to become law — but because it was the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot before time ran out." Evolve California, which also opposes Proposition 43, said, "If this measure passes, it will make California the hardest place in the country to raise local revenue."[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

## Prediction markets

*See also: [Prediction markets](/Prediction_markets "Prediction markets")*

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders. 

This section displays the contract prices on the outcome of this election from Kalshi, one of several prediction market platforms. Ballotpedia displays prediction market data for informational purposes; these markets do not predict election outcomes with certainty.

## Background

### General tax vs. special tax

[Section 1 of Article XIII C](/Article_XIII_C,_California_Constitution#Section_1 "Article XIII C, California Constitution") of the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution") defines a *general tax* as "any tax imposed for general governmental purposes." The section defines *special tax* as "any tax imposed for specific purposes, including a tax imposed for specific purposes, which is placed into a general fund." A *tax* is defined as "any levy, charge, or exaction of any kind imposed by a local government."[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) 

### California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)

*See also: [California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)](/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_\(June_1978\) "California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)")*

In 1978, California voters approved [Proposition 13](/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_\(June_1978\) "California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)") by a margin of 65% to 35%. The initiated constitutional amendment required local governments to refer special taxes to the ballot and required a two-thirds vote of electors. The amendment also:[\[13\]](#cite_note-taxdata-13) 

*   required that properties be taxed at no more than 1% of their full cash value shown on the 1975-1976 assessment rolls;
*   limited annual increases of assessed (taxable) value to the inflation rate or 2%, whichever was less;
*   allowed properties to be reassessed at 1% of their sale price upon property transfer and reset the limit on annual increases of assessed value;
*   prohibited the state legislature from enacting new taxes on the value or sale of properties;
*   require a two-thirds vote of the state legislature to increase non-property taxes; and
*   make the state government responsible for distributing property tax revenue among local governments.

[Howard Jarvis](/Howard_Jarvis "Howard Jarvis"), the founder of the [Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association](/Howard_Jarvis_Taxpayers_Association "Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association"), and Paul Gann, who developed the [Gann Limit](/California_Proposition_98,_Mandatory_Education_Spending_Initiative_\(1988\) "California Proposition 98, Mandatory Education Spending Initiative (1988)"), were proponents of the initiative.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) 

### California Proposition 218, Voter Approval Requirement for Local Tax Increases Initiative (1996)

*See also: [California Proposition 218 (1996)](#California_Proposition_218,_Voter_Approval_Requirement_for_Local_Tax_Increases_Initiative_\(1996\))*

In 1996, California voters approved Proposition 218 by a vote of 56.5% to 43.5%. Proposition 218 required local governments to refer ordinances to impose taxes or property-related assessments, fees, and charges to the ballot for voter consideration. It also required that elections for general taxes be held at regular elections and required a two-thirds supermajority vote of approval for special taxes. 

#### Lawsuits regarding Proposition 218 vote requirements

An August 2017 [California Supreme Court decision](/Laws_governing_local_ballot_measures_in_California#Taxes_imposed_by_citizen_initiatives "Laws governing local ballot measures in California") raised questions about how to interpret the constitutional voting requirements for special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives. 

California voters approved [Proposition 218](/California_Proposition_218,_Voter_Approval_Requirement_for_Local_Tax_Increases_Initiative_\(1996\) "California Proposition 218, Voter Approval Requirement for Local Tax Increases Initiative (1996)") in 1996, adding Article XIII C Voter Approval For Local Tax Levies to the California Constitution. The article includes the requirement that local governments may only enact, extend, or increase a special tax with a [two-thirds (66.67%) vote](/Supermajority_requirement "Supermajority requirement") of the electorate.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) Following the passage of Proposition 218, the two-thirds supermajority vote requirement was applied to legislative referrals, referendums, and citizen initiatives. 

In August 2017, however, the [California Supreme Court](/California_Supreme_Court "California Supreme Court") ruled in *California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland* that one requirement contained in Article XIII C—that general taxes must be put on the ballot during general elections—did not apply to citizen initiatives. The court categorized taxes imposed by citizen initiatives as separate from taxes imposed by local governments. This ruling brought the [two-thirds (66.67%) vote](/Supermajority_requirement "Supermajority requirement") requirement into question for special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives. 

City and county officials in San Francisco argued that the court's 2017 decision meant that a simple majority—not a two-thirds supermajority—was required for the approval of local citizen initiatives, including tax measures that designate funds for specific purposes. Based on those arguments, the city certified the measures as approved. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association filed a lawsuit against the city and county in August 2018, stating that the [Proposition C](/San_Francisco,_California,_Proposition_C,_Commercial_Rent_Tax_for_Childcare_and_Early_Education_\(June_2018\) "San Francisco, California, Proposition C, Commercial Rent Tax for Childcare and Early Education (June 2018)"), a commercial rent tax for childcare initiative, did not receive sufficient votes because it needed a two-thirds supermajority vote.[\[18\]](#cite_note-SFC-18) 

On January 27, 2021, the First District Court of Appeal ruled that the supermajority requirement did not apply to Proposition C and only applied to measures placed on the ballot by the city council, board of supervisors, or school board.[\[19\]](#cite_note-ruling-19) 

### California Two-Thirds Legislative Vote and Voter Approval for New or Increased Taxes Initiative (2024)

*See also: [California Two-Thirds Legislative Vote and Voter Approval for New or Increased Taxes Initiative (2024)](/California_Two-Thirds_Legislative_Vote_and_Voter_Approval_for_New_or_Increased_Taxes_Initiative_\(2024\) "California Two-Thirds Legislative Vote and Voter Approval for New or Increased Taxes Initiative (2024)")*

In 2024, the [Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association](/Howard_Jarvis_Taxpayers_Association "Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association") and California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative that would have amended the state constitution to define all state and local levies, charges, and fees as taxes and to require new state taxes proposed by the state legislature to be enacted via a two-thirds legislative vote and voter approval and new local taxes to be enacted via a two-thirds vote of the electorate.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) 

In June 2024, prior to the finalization of statewide ballots, the [California Supreme Court](/California_Supreme_Court "California Supreme Court") unanimously ruled that the 2024 initiative amounted to a revision of the state constitution and was therefore unconstitutional and could not go before voters in November.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) 

### California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)

*See also: [California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)](/California_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Special_Taxes_and_Charter_City_Real_Estate_Transfer_Tax_Prohibition_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)")*

The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and California Business Roundtable qualified a ballot initiative for the 2026 election cycle that was withdrawn from the ballot following a legislative compromise, which included the passage of [ACA 22](#Path_to_the_ballot) placing Proposition 43 on the November 3 ballot. The initiative would have amended the state constitution to increase the vote requirement to pass citizen-initiated local special taxes from a simple majority (50%+1) to a two-thirds (66.67%) vote; prohibited charter cities from imposing their own real estate transfer taxes, whether for general or specific purposes, above the existing statutory rate of $0.275 per $500 of value; and invalidated any property-related special taxes previously adopted with an approval rate below two-thirds or real estate transfer taxes in charter cities. ACA 22 is not retroactive like the withdrawn ballot initiative.[\[22\]](#cite_note-text-22) 

On June 25, 2026, the [California State Legislature](/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") passed ACA 22 and withdrew a [separate ballot measure](/California_Vote_Requirements_for_Initiatives_Requiring_Supermajority_Votes_Amendment_\(2026\) "California Vote Requirements for Initiatives Requiring Supermajority Votes Amendment (2026)") that had previously been referred to the 2026 ballot. It would have required initiatives proposing supermajority vote thresholds to pass by the same vote threshold being proposed.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

## How to cast a vote

*See also: [Voting in California](/Voting_in_California "Voting in California")*

*See below to learn more about current voter registration rules, identification requirements, and poll times in California.* 

How to vote in California

### Poll times

All polls in California are open from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Pacific Time. Anyone in line when the polls close must be allowed to vote.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) 

### Registration

*Check your voter registration status **[here](https://voterstatus.sos.ca.gov/).***

To vote in California, an individual must be a U.S. citizen and California resident, not currently serving a state or federal prison term for the conviction of a felony, and not currently found mentally incompetent to vote by a court. A voter must be at least 18 years of age on election day. [Pre-registration](/Youth_pre-registration_laws_by_state "Youth pre-registration laws by state") is available for 16 and 17-year-olds. Pre-registered voters are automatically registered to vote when they turn 18.[\[27\]](#cite_note-careg-27) 

### Automatic registration

*See also: [Automatic voter registration](/Automatic_voter_registration "Automatic voter registration")*

California [automatically](/Automatic_voter_registration "Automatic voter registration") registers eligible individuals to vote when they complete a driver's license, identification (ID) card, or change of address transaction through the Department of Motor Vehicles.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) 

### Online registration

*See also: [Online voter registration](/Online_voter_registration "Online voter registration")*

California has implemented an online voter registration system. Residents can register to vote by visiting [this website](https://registertovote.ca.gov/). 

### Same-day registration

*See also: [Same-day voter registration](/Same-day_voter_registration "Same-day voter registration")*

California allows [same-day voter registration](/Same-day_voter_registration "Same-day voter registration"). 

Californians must be registered to vote at least 15 days before election day. If the registration deadline has passed for an upcoming election, voters may visit a county elections office, polling place, or vote center during the 14 days prior to, and including election day to conditionally register to vote and vote a provisional ballot, which are counted once county election officials have completed the voter registration verification process. The state refers to this process as same day voter registration.[\[29\]](#cite_note-casdreg-29)[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) 

### Residency requirements

To register to vote in California, you must be a resident of the state. State law does not specify a length of time for which you must have been a resident to be eligible. 

### Verification of citizenship

*See also: [Laws permitting noncitizens to vote in the United States](/Laws_permitting_noncitizens_to_vote_in_the_United_States "Laws permitting noncitizens to vote in the United States")*

California's constitution requires that voters be U.S. citizens. When registering to vote, proof of citizenship is not required. Individuals who become U.S. citizens less than 15 days before an election must bring proof of citizenship to their county elections office to register to vote in that election. An individual applying to register to vote must attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of perjury.[\[29\]](#cite_note-casdreg-29) 

As of October 2026, two jurisdictions in California had [authorized noncitizen residents to vote](/Laws_permitting_noncitizens_to_vote_in_the_United_States "Laws permitting noncitizens to vote in the United States") for local board of education positions through local ballot measures. Only one of those jurisdictions, San Francisco, had implemented that law. Noncitizens voting for board of education positions must register to vote using a separate application from the state voter registration application.[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) 

All 49 states with voter registration systems require applicants to declare that they are U.S. citizens in order to register to vote in state and federal elections, under penalty of perjury or other punishment.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) Eight states — Alabama, Arizona, Kansas, Louisiana, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Utah, and Wyoming — have laws requiring individuals provide proof of citizenship at the time of voter registration, whether in effect or not. Three states, Florida, Georgia and Mississippi, require a person provide proof of citizenship if their citizenship status cannot be verified by other means.[\[33\]](#cite_note-33) One state, Ohio, requires proof of citizenship only when registering to vote at a Bureau of Motor Vehicles facility. In three states — California, Maryland, and Vermont — at least one local jurisdiction allows noncitizens to vote in some local elections. Noncitizens registering to vote in those elections must complete a voter registration application provided by the local jurisdiction and are not eligible to register as state or federal voters.

# CA 

Prop 43

| Constitutional Amendment

## Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services

Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.spur.org%2Fvoter-guide%2F2026-11%2Fca-prop-43-local-tax-threshold&title=California%20Prop%2043%20-%20Local%20Tax%20Threshold "Share on Facebook") [](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.spur.org%2Fvoter-guide%2F2026-11%2Fca-prop-43-local-tax-threshold&text=California%20Prop%2043%20-%20Local%20Tax%20Threshold "Share on Twitter") [](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.spur.org%2Fvoter-guide%2F2026-11%2Fca-prop-43-local-tax-threshold "Share on LinkedIn") [](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection# "Share via Email") 

### SPUR's Recommendation

SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.

##### Vote NO

![](/themes/custom/spur5/images/voter-guide/no-highlight.svg) 

## **What Prop. 43 Would Do**

Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.

Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.

## **The Backstory**

Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in *California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland* (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval.[1](#_ftn1) Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.

Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution.[2](#_ftn2) That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.

Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.

## **Equity Impacts**

Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.

Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.

## **Pros**

*   Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
*   The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).

## **Cons**

*   Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
*   The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
*   It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

City of Upland*, which distinguished citizen-initiated measures from those placed on the ballot by local governments. Lower courts subsequently ruled that special taxes (those dedicated to specific purposes) via citizen petition need only 50%+1, not two-thirds.[[1]](https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-43-local-special-tax)

Since 2017, roughly two dozen such measures have passed statewide with support below two-thirds, including parcel taxes, sales taxes, and others for parks, transit, housing, homelessness, and public safety. High-profile examples include Los Angeles Measure ULA (the "mansion tax") in 2022, which passed with 57.77%. Critics, including the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA), describe many as "sneaky workarounds" where local governments or allies craft the measure, fund polling/messaging, then "hand it off" to a citizens' group or special interest to collect signatures and qualify it as an initiative.[[2]](https://www.golden-state.org/supermajority-requirements-are-undemocratic-so-is-proposition-43/)

- **Santa Cruz Measure C (2025, housing/homelessness parcel and transfer tax)**: The City Council used public funds (~$35,000–$40,000) for polling and message testing. In a recorded May 9, 2023, council meeting, Mayor Fred Keeley discussed handing the measure off to a housing advocacy group (Housing Santa Cruz County) for a "path to a lower threshold," noting it "might make sense for the council to see if there is a way the public might consider advancing a bond measure to the ballot with the assistance of the city government." City staff helped with campaign infrastructure. Keeley (a major donor, contributing $50,000+) and the council supported it; it passed with about 54–56% (below two-thirds). Opponents called it a city-engineered "end around" using taxpayer-funded work. The city attorney deemed it legal as a citizen initiative.[[3]](https://www.santacruzsentinel.com/2025/09/17/guest-commentary-legal-loophole-behind-santa-cruz-housing-tax/)

- **San Francisco Proposition C (2018, business tax for homeless services)**: This citizen initiative (led by the group Our City Our Home) passed with 61.34%. Supervisor Norman Yee was a driving force—he submitted the signed petitions and signed ballot arguments. Courts (including the Court of Appeal) upheld it as a valid citizen initiative requiring only a majority, even with elected official involvement, distinguishing it from measures referred by the Board of Supervisors. Similar 2018 San Francisco measures were also treated this way. The city later validated it in court.[[4]](https://www.reubenlaw.com/proposition-c-upheld-by-court-of-appeal/)

- **Other cases**: Oakland Measure E (parcel tax, pushed by city employee unions with vague spending language). Crockett Measure L (parcel tax, ~63%). Various others involved unions, environmental groups, or homeless-services advocates. HJTA notes instances where governments draft measures, then special interests qualify them. In one case, the state (via AB 1923) required Fresno County to place a citizens' initiative sales tax on the ballot over local objections. Courts have generally allowed official involvement as long as the petition process is followed.[[5]](https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/citizens-initiative-tax-measures-under-scrutiny-due-to-only-needing-simple-majority/)

HJTA and taxpayer groups argue this lets special interests "write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves," and evade Prop 13/218. Supporters of the process (including some local officials and advocates) view it as legitimate use of the initiative power, with community input, and note that general taxes still need only a majority. Some measures have faced (or could face) legal challenges over public-fund use or government sponsorship.[[6]](https://aoausa.com/proposition-43-california-two-thirds-tax-rule/)

This "Upland loophole" prompted Proposition 43 (a 2026 legislative constitutional amendment, part of a deal with HJTA) to require two-thirds for *all* local special taxes, including citizen-initiated ones, starting January 1, 2027 (without retroactively invalidating prior ones). It would close the disparity. General taxes would remain at majority vote.[[7]](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5af07fd050a54f8fc370c748/t/6a987cb0022930285017990f/1788378288890/FINAL+Prop+43+Local+Taxes+Limitation.pdf)

# PROP 43: Two-Thirds Vote for Local Special Taxes

[Download PDF](<https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California Decides_Proposition 43.pdf>) 

[Research](#researchareas) 

*   [Quick Facts](#facts)
*   [Key Questions](#key-questions)
*   [Risks & Benefits](#risks)

[California Decides](https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides) 

###### Quick Facts

*   ​​​​​​**Official ballot title:** “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
*   **Type:** Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
*   **A vote YES means:** New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
*   **A vote NO means:** Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
*   **Sponsor/proponent:** Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
*   **On the ballot because:** The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
*   **Full legal text:** [ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
*   **LAO analysis:** [Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)

###### 1\. What would it do?

Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.

The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.

 

###### 2\. The legal language

*   **Full text:** [ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
*   **Key language:**

“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” \[1, Sec. 4.5(a)\]

*   **What it amends:** Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.

 

###### 3\. What, Where, When, Why?

*   **Who?** Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
*   **What?** A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
*   **Where?** Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
*   **When?** On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
*   **Why?** Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.

###### 4\. Trade-offs

For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.

The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.

There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.

## 5\. Potential risks and benefits

**Potential benefits**

*   It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
*   It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
*   It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
*   It adds certainty. Litigation since *Upland* left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.

**Potential risks**

*   It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
*   It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
*   It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
*   Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
*   The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.

## 6\. Open questions

*   How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
*   Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
*   Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
*   How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
*   With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?

###### 7\. The questions to ask before you vote

A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?

Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?
